status: candidate / pending_human_review (model reading, round 21 second round; not an operator gate)
dataset_family: Neurology clinic cohort, Sivas State Hospital and Bozok University School of Medicine (Yozgat), Turkey (ethics 2017-KAEK-189): 56 MCI + 50 age- and education-matched healthy volunteers aged 60-80. No other corpus block reports this sample.
method_family: Pattern-reversal VEP recorded from occipital scalp electrodes (O1/O2/Oz, reference Cz; Nihon Kohden Neuropack; monocular checkerboard stimulation to ISCEV standard). Group comparison by t-test or Mann-Whitney on five waveform measures per eye, plus Spearman correlations with MMSE subdomains. No classifier, no multiplicity correction.
what_it_shows:
Kisli M, Sacmaci H (2025), Behavioural Brain Research 484:115504.
- Of ten VEP comparisons (five measures x two eyes), one differed: left-eye P100 latency was 106.75 +/- 11.17 ms in MCI against 101.82 +/- 8.97 in controls, p = 0.027 unadjusted.
- All other pattern-VEP parameters, for both eyes, did not differ (p > 0.05).
- In MCI patients, right N75-P100 and P100-N145 amplitudes correlated with MMSE recall (rho 0.399 and 0.314).
why:
IDENTITY. The PDF's title, authors (Mesude Kisli, Hikmet Sacmaci) and DOI 10.1016/j.bbr.2025.115504 match the block header and author list. I read the whole extract, pp.1-5, up to the References.

STATED FORM, no. The statement names the ocular channels in its parenthesis: retinal structure and eye-movement behaviour. This study measures neither. A pattern-reversal VEP is a cortical evoked potential recorded from scalp electrodes over the occiput ('recorded from an effective electrode positioned on the occipital area', p.2). The eye is only the route of the stimulus, and the authors themselves describe P100 latency as reflecting 'conduction time to the occipital cortex' (p.3). It is a visual-pathway neurophysiology measure. It is not retinal structure and not eye-movement behaviour. Scalability and detection are not tested; there is no classifier or accuracy.

NARROWED FORM, no. Even under a broad reading of 'ocular measures' to mean any visual-system measure, the evidence does not show an association. The reasons below are my arithmetic or my reading of the source, not the authors' statements.
(1) Only one of ten comparisons reached p < 0.05, at p = 0.027, with no correction. A Bonferroni threshold for ten tests is 0.005. The same measure in the right eye did not differ (p = 0.118).
(2) The Results text says P100 latency 'significantly decreased in the patient group' (p.3). The abstract and Table 2 say it was longer (106.75 vs 101.82 ms). Table 2 supports 'longer', but the source contradicts itself.
(3) The degrees of freedom are printed as 84, although 106 participants are analysed.
(4) By the paper's own MMSE scheme, 24 or more is normal and 19-23 is 'mild' impairment, yet the MCI group's mean MMSE of 21.42 falls in that mild band (p.2; abstract). This casts doubt on the MCI case definition, as the finder also noted.
(5) Table 1's control gender ratio (33/20) adds to 53, not 50. The control recall median '0 (1-2)' lies outside its own IQR. Table 3 attributes the attention-N75 correlation to controls, while the text attributes it to patients.
The authors concede a cross-sectional design and no flash-VEP re-test, and they state that 'more study evidence is needed' (p.4).

If the operator nevertheless read 'ocular measures' as including visual evoked potentials, the most this study could give is partly, for a single unadjusted latency difference. That is not a yes on either form.

SCOPE NOTE. P-933, a round-1 candidate, also recorded PVEP and FERG. Its round-1 narrowed yes rests on OCT macular RNFL, not on VEP, so this verdict does not conflict with it.

INDEPENDENCE. Sivas and Yozgat, Turkey. No shared sample, site or authors with P-5, P-952, P-966 or P-105, or with the round-1 candidates. The finder notes it is distinct from P-686 (Izmir). Not a preprint: a peer-reviewed Elsevier article.

DEFECTS NOTED. The registry Modality 'MRI/PET' is wrong; the paper is pattern-reversal VEP, with MRI used only for exclusion. The registry Sample_N_Approx and the block's sample-size field both read 50; the PDF gives 106 (56 MCI + 50 controls).

quotes.quote: The groups consisted of 56 MCI and 50 healthy volunteers, aged 60–80 years, matched for age and education.
The mean MMSE score in the MCI group was 21.42 ± 1.55 points. Our findings showed that individuals with MCI had a longer left P100 latency compared to controls (p = 0.027).
A score of 24 or higher (out of 30) indicated normal cognition. However, scores under these might indicate severe (≤9 points), moderate (10–18 points), or mild (19–23 points).
VEPs were recorded from an effective electrode positioned on the occipital area in a manner where the reference electrode was on Cz (O1, O2, Oz).

According to the results, P100 wave latency significantly decreased in the patient group compared to the control group (df = 84, p = 0.027) in the area where the sinistral eye Oz electrode was present. Moreover, other pattern-VEP parameters regarding both eyes did not display a statistical difference in patient and control groups (p > 0.05, others).
VEP Pl00 latency is thought to reflect conduction time to the occipital cortex, but disruption of visual pathways prior to the occipital area may also contribute to prolongation of Pl00 latency
Patient’s Recall- Right N75-P100 amplitude 0.399 0.011 Patient’s Recall- Right P100-N145 amplitude 0.314 0.049 Control’s Attention- Right N75 latency 0.357 0.030

The limitation of the study was that the pattern VEP responses were not re-tested using the flash VEP. The method was cross-sectional, and the patients who applied owing to dementia and their clinic were not observed in the long term using the neuro-physiological tests.
Nevertheless, more study evidence is needed to confirm the use of VEP in clinical environments.
